title: The forgetting curve. It came from one man memorising nonsense.
description:
It came from one man memorising nonsense. Hermann Ebbinghaus was the only subject in his own experiments, reported in 1885.

Learned lists of meaningless syllables, then measured how much effort it took to relearn them later.

In each list of the 2015 replication, set out in rows of 13.

On himself. At the University of Amsterdam, Joeri Dros, a 22 year old, was the only subject. It took about 70 hours.

The curve held up. It closely matched Ebbinghaus's data. Only the 31 day score came out much lower.

Memory rose after a day. The authors saw a likely jump from the 24 hour point, which sleep research would predict. The paper does not prove sleep caused it.

Two men, 130 years apart, one curve.

Sources:
- https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0120644 (read, first 100000 characters): Murre and Dros, PLOS ONE 2015; established that Hermann Ebbinghaus was the only subject in his own experiments, reported in 1880 and 1885; that the replication at the University of Amsterdam had one subject, Joeri Dros, a 22 year old man; that it ran 1 December 2011 to 13 February 2012 and took about 70 hours; that each list held 104 nonsense syllables in 8 rows of 13; that relearning was tested after 20 minutes, 1 hour, 9 hours, 1 day, 2 days, 6 days and 31 days; that the curve closely resembled Ebbinghaus's data; that the 31 day score was much lower; and that a likely upward jump from the 24 hour point is what sleep research would predict, without the paper establishing a sleep cause.
